rows.title: Parliamentary Committees
rows.text: Parliamentary committees convert episodic floor accountability into continuous, specialised and relatively deliberative scrutiny of legislation, expenditure and administration.

rows.title: Advisory recommendations
rows.text: Committee recommendations generally lack binding force, weakening implementation where executive follow-through is poor.

rows.title: Deliberative space
rows.text: Smaller cross-party forums permit less adversarial and more detailed discussion than the full House.

rows.title: Continuous executive accountability
rows.text: Ministries and officials face detailed examination beyond episodic floor mechanisms, extending parliamentary oversight.

rows.title: Complementary financial scrutiny
rows.text: PAC examines propriety of expenditure, Estimates Committee stresses economy and efficiency, while COPU scrutinises public enterprises.

rows.title: Financial accountability
rows.text: PAC, Estimates Committee and COPU operationalise Parliament's power of the purse through complementary scrutiny.

rows.title: Declining referral
rows.text: When major Bills bypass committee scrutiny, Parliament loses an important stage of detailed legislative examination.

rows.title: Presumptive Bill referral
rows.text: Significant non-urgent Bills should ordinarily undergo committee scrutiny before final passage.

rows.title: Research-capacity deficit
rows.text: Limited dedicated expert support constrains scrutiny of increasingly technical legislation and policy.

rows.title: Professional committee support
rows.text: Permanent research and domain expertise can strengthen continuity, technical scrutiny and institutional memory.

rows.title: Weak institutional memory
rows.text: Short committee tenure limits continuity and accumulation of subject expertise.

rows.title: Legislative specialisation
rows.text: Repeated sectoral exposure develops domain familiarity among MPs and narrows the legislature–executive information gap.

rows.title: Specialised scrutiny
rows.text: Detailed ministry- and subject-specific examination compensates for limited floor time and improves legislative scrutiny.

rows.title: Standing and ad hoc committees
rows.text: The committee system combines permanent standing bodies with issue- or Bill-specific ad hoc committees.

rows.title: Bill referral during the 17th Lok Sabha
rows.text: Declining committee referral is relevant evidence when evaluating the effectiveness of legislative scrutiny. Supports the limitation that formal committee capacity matters only when Bills are actually referred.

rows.title: Motor Vehicles Bill committee scrutiny
rows.text: Committee scrutiny of major legislation can demonstrate how detailed examination improves a Bill. Use only to strengthen the specialised-scrutiny argument after checking the underlying committee record.

rows.title: 2017 · 10 marks
rows.text: Discuss the role of Public Accounts Committee in establishing accountability of the government to the people.

rows.title: 2018 · 10 marks
rows.text: Why do you think the committees are considered to be useful for parliamentary work? Discuss, in this context, the role or the Estimates Committee.

rows.title: 2021 · 15 marks
rows.text: Do Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees keep the administration on its toes and inspire reverence for parliamentary control? Evaluate the working of such committees with suitable examples.

rows.title: 2023 · 15 marks
rows.text: Explain the structure of the Parliamentary Committee system. How far have the financial committees helped in the institutionalization of Indian Parliament?

rows.title: Institutional burden sharing
rows.text: Delegating technical scrutiny to smaller bodies frees floor time without surrendering parliamentary oversight.

rows.title: Expert and stakeholder input
rows.text: Committees can obtain specialised testimony and official evidence, making legislative examination more evidence-based.

rows.title: Weak follow-through
rows.text: Insufficient floor discussion and action on committee findings may reduce their institutional influence.
